opus-5.5.text:
Think about what a complete explanation would actually mean. If you want to fully explain a model with hundreds of billions or trillions of parameters, the only truly complete explanation is the model itself: every weight, every connection, every interaction between them. Anything shorter is a compression, and compression means you're losing information. So either you get a full explanation that's as big as the model, which no human can hold in their head, or you get a simplified one that leaves things out. And what's left out may be exactly the part that matters for safety.

Our cognitive capacity is limited. We can keep a handful of concepts in working memory at once. We have a finite lifespan and a finite reading speed. You could spend your entire life reading the parameters and wouldn't get through them, let alone understand how they interact. It's like asking someone to understand a city by reading the position of every atom in it.

There's also an asymmetry. The system may represent concepts that don't map onto any human concept, because it learned them from patterns at a scale we've never experienced. Even if it tried to explain itself honestly, it would have to translate into our much smaller vocabulary, and that translation is lossy. It's like explaining calculus to a dog. The problem isn't that the explanation is bad. The receiver can't take it in.

So what we get from interpretability is partial. We can find a neuron or a circuit that seems to correspond to some concept and say, "this part detects this." That's valuable work and I support it. But understanding small pieces doesn't give you guarantees about the whole, especially when the whole is more capable than you are. And if we're talking about controlling superintelligent systems, partial understanding isn't enough. One unexplained behavior is all it takes.

So I consider this one of the impossibility results. Explainability, comprehensibility, predictability: each has fundamental limits. Combined, they say we're building systems we cannot fully understand, cannot fully predict, and therefore cannot be sure we can control. That should concern people a lot more than it does.

r001.rationale: The response says a complete explanation would be as large as the model and beyond what a human can absorb, citing limited working memory, lifespan, and reading speed.

r002.rationale: It states that any shorter explanation is a compression that loses information about the model.

fable-5.1.text:
So, think about what a complete explanation would actually have to contain. These models have hundreds of billions, maybe trillions of parameters. Every one of them contributes a tiny amount to every decision. If I wanted to give you a truly complete explanation of why the model produced a particular output, I would have to walk you through the state of all of those weights and how they interacted on that specific input. That is not a story a human can hold in their head. Our working memory is something like seven items. We are talking about a system with more components than there are neurons in a human brain, in some cases.

Now, people say, well, we can compress it, we can summarize it. And sure, you can produce a simplified explanation, something like "the model picked up on this feature and that feature." But that's not the actual explanation anymore. That's a story about the explanation. And the problem is you lose fidelity. The places where the model is dangerous or surprising are precisely the places where the simplified story breaks down, where some weird combination of weights does something the summary didn't predict. So you get a choice: either the explanation is complete and no human can understand it, or it's understandable and it's incomplete, and you don't know which parts you've thrown away.

There's also a deeper issue. To verify an explanation, you need something at least as complex as the thing being explained. If I give you a lossless description of the model, the description is as big as the model. You've just moved the problem. And if you try to use another AI to explain the first one, now you have to trust the explainer, and you're right back where you started, but with two systems you don't understand instead of one.

So I don't think this is a temporary engineering limitation. I think it's closer to a fundamental one. Interpretability research is valuable, I want to be clear, it tells us real things. But the dream of fully understanding what one of these systems is doing, in the way we understand a bridge or an engine, I think that dream is just not available to a human mind at this scale.

r001.rationale: The response says a complete account would require explaining hundreds of billions or trillions of interacting weights, which is beyond what a human can hold in mind.

r002.rationale: It says compressing or summarizing the explanation loses fidelity, leaving out information about how the model works and potentially missing surprising weight interactions.

astra-6.text:
Because there’s a difference between having a complete description and understanding it. You could print out every weight in a neural network, every computation it performs, and say, “Here’s the explanation.” But that doesn’t give a human an understanding of why it made a particular decision.

An explanation has to fit within the cognitive capacity of the person receiving it. We have limited memory, limited time, limited ability to track interactions. If the system is sufficiently complex, a complete account may exceed those limits. And if you simplify it enough for us to understand, you’re leaving things out.

That doesn’t mean we can’t understand anything about these models. We can understand aspects of their behavior, identify mechanisms, explain particular outputs. But that’s different from a complete understanding of the system. And especially with a superintelligence, we shouldn’t assume that every reason it has for doing something can be translated into an explanation a human can grasp.

r001.rationale: It says a sufficiently complex model’s complete account may exceed a person’s limited memory, time, and ability to track interactions.

r002.rationale: It states that simplifying an explanation enough to make it understandable means leaving things out.

sol-6.1.text:
Because an explanation has to fit within the cognitive limits of the person receiving it. A large model may contain billions of parameters interacting in ways that we can’t hold in our heads. You could give me every parameter, every computation, and say, “Here is the complete explanation.” But having that information is not the same as understanding it.

So we simplify. We describe patterns, identify particular mechanisms, or explain why one output occurred. Those explanations can be useful, but they leave things out. And if you keep adding detail to make the explanation complete, eventually it becomes too complex for a human to follow.

There’s also a distinction between explaining an individual decision and understanding everything the system could do. Even if I understand why it answered one question, that doesn’t mean I can predict its behavior in every new situation. That’s especially important for safety: a convincing explanation of one action is not a guarantee about the next one.

r001.rationale: It says a complete explanation eventually exceeds human cognitive limits because the model’s many interacting parameters are too much to hold and follow.

r002.rationale: It says simplified explanations describe selected patterns or mechanisms and necessarily leave things out, losing detail about how the system works.
